item.title: Solid-state emissive acceptors enable thermally accessible radiative pathways for efficient organic solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02009-8 Solid-state emissive guest acceptors enhance organic solar cells by establishing thermally accessible radiative pathways, significantly reducing non-radiative voltage loss end enabling ternary blend devices with a certified power conversion efficiency of 20.84%.

item.title: Stable deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes with reduced efficiency roll-off via accelerated exciton utilization
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02029-4 Deep-blue organic light-emitting diodes leveraging phosphor-assisted TADF-sensitized fluorescence enable accelerated exciton dynamics, resulting in devices with an external quantum efficiency of 35.9% and an LT80 lifetime of 632 h.

item.title: Phase control of interfering stimulated Raman pathways in the XUV regime
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02024-9 Researchers modulate population transfer from the helium ground state to a metastable state by controlling the relative phase between two interfering stimulated Raman pathways through the continuum, demonstrating phase-coherent control in the extreme ultraviolet.

item.title: High-entropy molecular contacts enable high-efficiency and stable perovskite solar cells
item.description: Nature Photonics, Published online: 09 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41566-026-02028-5 High-entropy molecular contacts made by blending self-assembled molecules improve hole transport through diverse packing modes. Solar cells incorporating these contacts achieve a certified power conversion efficiency of 27.31% and negligible loss after 1,300 h of operation at 85 °C.

item.title: Software advance brings complex quantum simulations to standard computers
item.description: A major software advance could aid the creation of bigger, more reliable quantum computers, a study suggests. Researchers have developed an algorithm that enables off-the-shelf computers to run quantum simulations previously only possible using the world's most powerful supercomputers.

item.title: Jamming the flow to enable memory in quantum materials
item.description: Understanding and controlling phase transitions are fundamental to physics and central to many technological revolutions. There is currently strong interest in materials with coupled structural and electronic phase transitions, where controlling the transition plasticity naturally yields built-in memory—a key step in emulating neurons and synapses for "neuromorphic" or brain-like computing technologies.

item.title: Quantum physicists trace a century of controlling spin
item.description: A concept from the field of quantum mechanics, spin is a property of particles that has no direct counterpart in everyday experience. Since the early 20th century, researchers have learned to manipulate it deliberately by means of precisely shaped electromagnetic pulses. item.title: New stability rules distinguish quantum phases of matter that an older method wrongly groups together
item.description: Most of us recognize basic phases of matter and their properties: solids maintain their shape, liquids flow freely with constant volume, and gases expand to fill their container. Quantum phases, on the other hand, are much harder to categorize, overturning traditional notions of what a phase even is and forcing physicists to rethink their definitions.

item.title: Hybrid quantum computer observes foundational quantum effect in a new setting
item.description: Physicists in the Department of Physics at the University of Oxford have used a hybrid quantum computer, made up of qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation. The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by traveling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

item.title: Quantum chip holds multiple photons at once, opening path to scalable memory
item.description: For highly fragile quantum information systems, the ability to store quantum information is vital—but also challenging. Quantum information is transported in particles of light called photons, which often must be temporarily paused (or "stored") while other, slower quantum operations catch up. This storage must be performed on microchips as small as 1 centimeter (0.4 inches)—a distance covered by light in a few trillionths of a second.
